blocks: In this garden, Backblaze B2 Asset pages represent files stored in Backblaze B2, following Logseq/Entity/Asset for filenames, ownership, and page contents.
Upload the page-derived filename at the root of the garden's configured B2 bucket. Its optional local copy uses assets/.remote/<filename>.
For Course/Asset/Diagram/Overview/png, the filename is Course___Asset___Diagram___Overview.png and the local copy is assets/.remote/Course___Asset___Diagram___Overview.png.

Public uploads use the S3 endpoint returned by B2 authorization: https://<s3-host>/<garden-bucket>/Course___Asset___Diagram___Overview.png. The garden's B2 configuration supplies the host and bucket; URL encoding preserves the filename.
Private uploads retain the authenticated B2 download URL, https://<download-host>/file/<garden-bucket>/<filename>.
The body uses the usable remote URL. The URL already identifies the bucket and filename; separate properties would repeat them.
Uploading makes a file available at its remote location. Publication through a website or podcast feed is a separate step in that site's workflow.
DVC maintains checksums and restoration metadata separately. A DVC push backs up a tracked file; a named B2 upload supplies the URL used by its asset page.
tracks the page-named working file; backs it up and restores it. uploads and verifies the named object used by the page.
The measured playback length of an audio or video asset, in seconds.
A positive number, with fractional seconds allowed. For example, duration-seconds:: 757.761066.
Optional for audio and video assets; omitted for files without a playback duration.

Book pages are published works. They are usually tracked under Person/<name>/Book/YY/<short title>. They may be at Book/YY/<short title> if there are five or more sub-pages to the namespace or if the book has more than one author.
A book that is also a member of a sequence is both a Book and a Logseq/Entity/Series instance. Its path then interposes Series/<Series Name> after Book, per that type page.
Mark instances with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Book]] so this type page collects backlinks to every book entity.
When the author is clear, set created-by:: [[Person/Full Name]], [[Person/Full Name 2]] in frontmatter and ensure that person entity is in the garden.

The publication year is usually already carried in the page's own namespace segment (the YY in Person/<name>/Book/YY/<short title>), but that text is not a link. Optional: logseq-created-time-year:: linking to the matching instance makes it one.
H1 with the book’s title, linking to the book
In this garden, Book Section pages model one headed part of a book or manual as a navigable Logseq page.

A section has a distinct heading in the source and enough content to read or navigate independently. A caption, callout, paragraph, or table row stays inside its section rather than becoming a section page.

Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 1, Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 2, Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 3, and Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 4 specify the depth. The instance declares its most specific level in logseq-entity::; the level page points here for the shared shape.

A section is identified by its source work and its place in the heading tree. Search the intended path, aliases, and existing section content before creating a page; a changed heading or shortened title does not make a second section.

Nest each section under its parent page. Prefix each segment with a two-digit sibling order from the source, followed by a short, recognizable heading. Shorten long heading words where the meaning stays clear. The full source heading belongs in the page's H1, with its source number where useful.
Number siblings in source order, including unnumbered headings that qualify as sections. Keep the number local to the parent: 06 Dig Osc/02 Param Controls, then 02 Param Controls/01 Knob Speed.

Use the level-specific logseq-entity:: marker. up:: links to the parent page; prev:: and next:: link to adjacent siblings when those pages exist. The first and last sibling need only the available direction. See Logseq/Frontmatter for shared frontmatter conventions.

Begin with one bullet-wrapped H1. Put the section's own content under it in source order. Embed each imported child page once at the point where its heading occurs. The child page holds the text; the parent does not repeat it.

The Logseq user interface becomes messy-looking and sluggish when more than two levels of pages are embedded and are visible on a single page. It's okay if page MyPage has {{embed [[MyPage/MySubPage]]}}, and if MySubPage has {{embed [[MyPage/MySubPage/MySubSubPage]]}}, in it. It could be okay if there's only a single embed goes deeper and it's a very small page. But if the nesting goes deeper than that, it's usually a poor experience for the page viewer. As a convention, we permit embeds of L2 in L1 and L3 in L2, and use typical logseq wikilinks to L4.
A top-level Logseq/Entity/Book entity or a parent page of a Level 1 page has links to Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 1 sections, not embeds.

Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 1 has an embed of Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 2, and Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 2 has an embed of Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 3. Beneath that, it uses links to Logseq/Entity/Book/Section/Level 4.
Use Block References deeper than Level 4
If a page has a section like 1.2.3.4.5, then 5 should be a heading on the level 4 page. If another page references 1.2.3.4.5, then a
Use Block References deeper than Level 4
A newly available child appears in its parent's embed list, and adjacent sibling pages link in both directions through prev:: and next:: once both exist.

Turn the source's paragraphs, bullets, callouts, figures, and tables into readable nested blocks. Preserve the information needed to use the material, not the PDF's line wrapping or table grid. Use > [[Note/Info]] or > [[Note/Warning]] for corresponding callouts.

Place a figure under its caption block. Represent the image with a Logseq/Entity/Asset/B2 page beneath its owning section; Logseq/Entity/Asset defines its page-derived filename. Embed the verified remote URL with the caption as alt text. Keep the full PDF outside the graph.

Replace page-number references with a link to the corresponding section when it exists and its identity is clear. Otherwise, name the destination in prose without a speculative link. Do not preserve a bare PDF page number as navigation.

Compare the extracted text and images against the source pages: heading order, callout scope, figure/caption pairing, and cross-references can be lost in PDF extraction. The imported page should read naturally in Logseq and nvim.
Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/02 Param Controls and its child Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/02 Param Controls/01 Knob Speed show a callout and nested section.
In this garden, Book Section Level 1 pages model the topmost numbered parts of a book or manual.
A Level 1 page sits directly under the work's root page. Its two-digit prefix follows the source's chapter order; its H1 retains the chapter number and full heading.
It contains the chapter's introductory material and embeds its Level 2 children in reading order. An empty chapter shell is unnecessary when the chapter has not been imported.
The shared section shape lives on Logseq/Entity/Book/Section. Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc is an example.
In this garden, Book Section Level 2 pages model sections directly beneath a book's topmost part.
A Level 2 page sits under its Level 1 parent. Its two-digit prefix orders siblings within that parent; its H1 retains the source section number and heading when present.
It holds its own introductory material and embeds any Level 3 children at their source positions. Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/02 Param Controls is an example.
The shared section shape lives on Logseq/Entity/Book/Section.
In this garden, Book Section Level 3 pages model sections directly beneath a Level 2 section.
A Level 3 page sits under its Level 2 parent. Its two-digit prefix orders siblings within that parent; its H1 retains the source subsection number and heading when present.
It holds its own content and embeds any Level 4 children at their source positions. Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/02 Param Controls/01 Knob Speed is an example.
The shared section shape lives on Logseq/Entity/Book/Section.
In this garden, Book Section Level 4 pages model distinct headed sections directly beneath a Level 3 section.

A Level 4 page sits under its Level 3 parent. Its two-digit prefix orders siblings within that parent, even when the source leaves the heading unnumbered; its H1 retains the source heading and any source number.
A Level 4 page holds its own content. Smaller headings remain nested blocks within it unless the source hierarchy genuinely continues beyond this model.
The shared section shape lives on Logseq/Entity/Book/Section.
In this garden, Book User Guide pages model published instructions for using a particular item.
Place the guide at <Item>/UG, where <Item> is the page for the product or tool. One guide belongs to one item; search that namespace before creating another.
The guide page uses logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Book/User Guide]], [[Logseq/Entity/Book]]. It follows the shared book shape on Logseq/Entity/Book.
Place guide sections beneath <Item>/UG as Logseq/Entity/Book/Section instances. Their level, order, navigation, and page shape follow the level-specific section definitions.
The guide root links to its Level 1 sections in reading order; section content stays on the section pages.
Microfreak/UG contains the Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc section.
Each Entity Definition page describes a type of real-world entity that may be tracked in a page page. Entity here means something roughly analagous
, uniquely modeled in each garden are.
the garden tracks — each describes how to recognize, name, deduplicate, and shape instances of one kind of entity.

entity-proxy-source-properties:: lists property keys that an instance’s source garden controls, even when another entity definition gives those keys to the destination. This explicit source declaration takes precedence over entity-proxy-destination-properties::.

Re-sync updates, adds, or removes these properties to match the source. Removing a source property also removes the destination’s value. Protected tags:: and sync-owned proxy metadata cannot be assigned to the source through this declaration.
, Logseq/Entity/Software/Project, Logseq/Entity/Book, and the other pages under the Logseq/Entity/ namespace.
What counts as an Entity Definition
A page under the Logseq/Entity/ namespace whose job is to define one entity type: what counts as an instance, what does not, how to name and deduplicate it, and what shape its instance pages take.
What counts as an Entity Definition
Not an Entity Definition: an instance page (an actual person, project, book, …), or Logseq/Entity itself, which is the general conceptual model rather than a single type.
What counts as an Entity Definition

Frontmatter — logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Definition]] marks the page as an entity definition, so this page collects a backlink to every entity type. Add alias:: for plural or contextual forms when useful. Never alter tags::.

H1 — a single bullet-wrapped heading in human-friendly Title Case, with abbreviations expanded and no namespace path: - # Software Plugin, - # Security Vulnerability, - # CLI Command. The page's namespace already carries it.

First line — one sentence directly under the H1 in the form In this garden, **<Name>** pages model <description>. These first lines read together as a self-describing index of the garden's entity types.
Body sections — describe what is specific to recognizing, naming, deduplicating, and shaping that type. Adapt to the type; short definitions do not need every section. Common sections:
what counts as an instance, and what does not

Keep shared conventions on Logseq/Frontmatter and rather than repeating them on each type page.

entity-tasks:: declares the reference pages needed to work with instances of this entity. The property is a comma-separated list of wikilinks in the definition's frontmatter; an absent property declares no companion tasks.

follows an instance's logseq-entity:: links, imports its entity definitions, and follows each definition's entity-tasks:: links. Task references declare their executable files and required task dependencies through the companion-file contract on .
Shared entity definitions and task dependencies are visited once per sync. Cyclic relationships are allowed and terminate after their pages have been visited.

A referenced entity definition with no source file is reported as a logical page. A declared companion task or task dependency requires a source reference page and its mapped implementation files; missing task content stops application.

entity-proxy-destination-properties:: names, as a comma-separated list of property keys, the properties on an instance that belong to the garden holding a of it rather than to the source page. Re-syncing that proxy keeps the destination's values for them. An absent property names none.
For example, names podcast-guid and podcast-published-at, which the publishing garden records.

Logseq/Entity is the general conceptual model — what an entity is and how any page is marked as one. This page is the entity type whose instances are the definition pages themselves, so the garden's set of entity types is queryable through its backlinks rather than kept as a hand-maintained list.

In this garden, Diataxis Explanation pages model understanding-oriented writing: why something is the way it is, and how ideas fit together. They explain why and serve understanding, the reflective quadrant of .
A page that gives background, weighs alternatives, or draws the connections between ideas, rather than instructing or cataloguing.
Not an instance: a page of steps — or . A systematic description of a thing — .
This quadrant overlaps the entity system almost entirely: an explanation-shaped page in this garden is normally a concept instance, and governs its frontmatter, its naming, and its body sections.
Read first, then this page for the Diataxis vocabulary and the tag. Where the two differ, the Concept page wins on shape and this page wins on which quadrant the writing belongs to.
covers the narrower case of naming a thing rather than explaining it; a page can be both.
No namespace segment of its own — an explanation page is named for the idea it explains, wherever that idea naturally sits, per .
tags:: — new pages of this kind carry [[Diataxis/Concept]] (or [[Diataxis/Explanation]], the same cluster by alias). Add it on creation; never remove or rewrite tags on a page you did not create.
see-also:: — preferred over a ## Related section listing internal wikilinks.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Per . This type adds no shape of its own.
Take a wider view than a task allows: the history, the alternatives that were not taken, the reasons behind a design.
Admit the disagreements. Explanation is the one quadrant where opinion belongs, provided it is marked as such.
Link out to the how-to, tutorial and reference pages rather than absorbing their jobs.
The four Diataxis types are mutually exclusive in intent even when a topic needs all four; pick by what the reader needs, not by what is easiest to write.
— the framework concept page this type implements.

Logseq/Entity/Discussion — a Discussion page that weighs alternatives also carries this entity, after Discussion in its logseq-entity:: line. It takes its name, placement, shape and frontmatter from the Discussion definition, so an agent writing one leaves out the [[Diataxis/Concept]] tag that new Explanation pages otherwise carry.

In this garden, Discussion pages model the reasoning behind one subject page: the principles that shaped it, the alternatives weighed and the history of decisions about it. The subject page keeps only what is true of the subject.
A page at <Subject>/Discussion whose content is the reasoning behind <Subject>: why the subject is shaped the way it is, what else was considered, and what was decided when.

The subject can be any page: an entity definition such as Logseq/Entity/Music/Scale, a principle such as , or a preference such as . The subject page may exist only as a logical page, as Logseq/Entity/Hierarchy does.
Not an instance: a page about a conversation held somewhere else. A GitHub Discussions thread or a community forum thread is a , even when its path contains Discussion, as does.
Not an instance: a dated analysis nested under a Discussion page. It is an entry of that Discussion, described below.
One Discussion page per subject, at <Subject>/Discussion: discusses Logseq/Entity/Definition.
The subject page links its Discussion in see-also::.
Logseq/Frontmatter/logseq-entity should include the Logseq/Entity/Discussion, as per Logseq/Entity standards.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.

H1 — the subject page's H1 followed by Discussion: - # Music Scale Discussion for Logseq/Entity/Music/Scale, whose H1 is Music Scale. When the subject has no page file, the H1 names the subject in Title Case without the Logseq/ prefix, as - # Entity Hierarchy Discussion does for Logseq/Entity/Hierarchy. keeps the H1 codekiln wrote for it.
First line — one sentence directly under the H1 naming the questions the page covers.

Sections — one ## heading per decision or question, stating the choice or the question in plain words. Under each: the choice, the reasons for it, and the alternatives weighed with what each would cost. Optional sections: ## History for decisions in date order, each with its date as a journal date link such as ; ## Open questions for decisions not yet made.
Years — every year, decade or century in the text links to its page, named by digit groups: the year 1547 is and the twentieth century is , written in a sentence as [twentieth century]([[19]]).
Entries — a ## Entries section when the Discussion has dated analyses, described below.
A Discussion page may hold only its first line and its ## Entries section, as does.
An analysis is one author's written reasoning about the subject at one time, usually an AI model's. Each analysis has its own page, nested under the Discussion it belongs to:
An analysis is one author's written reasoning about the subject at one time, usually an AI model's. Each analysis has its own page, nested under the Discussion
<Model> is the last segment of the author's page: Opus for , Fable for .
An analysis is one author's written reasoning about the subject at one time, usually an AI model's. Each analysis has its own page, nested under the Discussion
YY/MM/DD is the two-digit year, month and day the analysis was written, and HHMM ET the 24-hour Eastern time.
An analysis is one author's written reasoning about the subject at one time, usually an AI model's. Each analysis has its own page, nested under the Discussion
<slug> states the analysis's main claim as a short sentence: Mark each page with the most specific entity in each lineage.
An analysis is one author's written reasoning about the subject at one time, usually an AI model's. Each analysis has its own page, nested under the Discussion

The analysis page carries author:: linking the author's AI Model page, and may carry see-also::. Its H1 repeats the slug, and its body has one ## heading per decision or question, as a Discussion page does.

The Discussion page lists each analysis under ## Entries, oldest first, under one ### heading for each day, time and model, such as ### [[2026-10-01 Thu]] 0611 ET Opus. Under that heading, one bullet per analysis gives the link to the analysis page, a hyphen, and one sentence summarizing the analysis.
codekiln's response to an entry nests under that entry's bullet.
is the worked example: its entry for links , and a nested bullet records the property codekiln proposed while reviewing it.

A Discussion page whose sections give reasons, history and the alternatives weighed is also a Diataxis Explanation, and lists Discussion first: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Discussion]], [[Logseq/Entity/Diataxis/Explanation]].

The Discussion definition sets the page's name, placement, shape and frontmatter. An agent writing a Discussion page leaves out tags::, including the [[Diataxis/Concept]] tag the Explanation definition asks for, because the always-on logseq-core rule bars agents from adding, changing or removing tags:: on any page.
A Discussion page made only of entries carries Discussion alone.

In this garden, Frontmatter Definition pages model a custom frontmatter property that one entity type adds for its instances — the property's meaning, its permitted values, and how instances set it. Global, cross-type conventions stay on Logseq/Frontmatter; a Frontmatter Definition is scoped to a single entity type.
A page whose job is to define one custom property belonging to a single entity type: what the property means, which values are permitted, and how an instance uses it.

Not an instance: a shared convention on Logseq/Frontmatter (those apply to every page, not one type); a Logseq/Entity/Definition page (that defines an entity type, not a property); an individual permitted value.
Ownership follows the namespace: Logseq/Entity/<Type>/Frontmatter/<key> belongs to Logseq/Entity/<Type>. A separate ownership property or body section would repeat that relationship.

A Frontmatter Definition lives under its owning type at Logseq/Entity/<Type>/Frontmatter/<key>, where <key> is the literal frontmatter key it defines, in kebab-case to match the :: property (for example dotfiles-dep-stage).
The /Frontmatter/ segment is the boundary: above it is the entity definition; at and below it are that type's frontmatter schema and values.

When the property draws from a closed set, enumerate the permitted values as child pages Logseq/Entity/<Type>/Frontmatter/<key>/<Value>. An instance references a value page, which gives autocomplete and turns each value page's linked references into the list of instances currently holding that value.

Value pages are permitted values, not definitions and not entities: they carry no logseq-entity::. An ordered vocabulary uses a leading number so the sequence sorts in order, for example 1 - Incubating.
On instances, set logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Frontmatter/Definition]] so this type page collects a backlink to every custom frontmatter property in the garden.

On instances, set alias:: [[<key>]] to the literal key the page defines, as alias:: [[logseq-entity-hierarchy-type]] on . Clicking a key in <key>:: <value> opens the page [[<key>]], and the alias makes that page the definition.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.

Logseq Flavored Markdown. Suggested sections: the property's meaning, its permitted values (link the value pages, in order), any rules between values, and ownership when the namespace does not already identify it.
Logseq/Entity/Definition — defines entity types; a Frontmatter Definition defines one property a type adds. A type page links its Frontmatter Definitions from its own ## Frontmatter section.
— a Frontmatter Definition is a schema: a declared shape a property's value must satisfy to count as valid.

In this garden, Musical Form pages model a named kind of composition that works across composers share, such as the prelude, the nocturne or the fugue, and the structural forms such as ternary or sonata form.
A named kind of piece or structure that more than one composer has written in. The page describes the form itself, apart from any one work.
A named kind of piece and the structure of the same name get sibling pages, Music/Form/Sonata and Music/Form/Sonata Form.
A work's title alone does not make a form: the Morceaux de fantaisie are not fantasias.
A form lives at Music/Form/<Name>, under , using its common English name in the singular, as .

A Logseq/Entity/Music/Work page links each of its forms with music-form::, defined at Logseq/Entity/Music/Work/Frontmatter/music-form. Those links are the form's list of works, so a form page lists works only to add notes about them.
A form page's linked references filtered by a composer's page show that composer's works in the form, since a work page's created-by:: sits in the same frontmatter block as its music-form::.
Start each form page with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Music/Form]] and one H1 with the form's common name.
Follow with a short description of the form and its history.
Why musical forms get pages of their own, why one Music/Form/ namespace holds both kinds of piece and structures, and why the garden does not model genre.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works

A form page gathers every work in that form across composers. lists every prelude in the garden in its linked references, and filtering those references by a composer's page narrows the list to that composer's preludes.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works

Each work page links its form with music-form::, defined at Logseq/Entity/Music/Work/Frontmatter/music-form. The filter works because music-form:: and created-by:: sit in the same frontmatter block, so no query is needed.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works
The pattern follows Logseq/Entity/Music/Scale: concept pages under Music/<Concept>/<Name> with an index page above them.
Forms get their own pages, linked from works
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures

"Sonata" names two related things. A sonata is a kind of piece, usually in several movements. Sonata form is the plan of a single movement: exposition, development, recapitulation. The second movement of Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata belongs to a sonata and is a rondo; the first movement of Mozart's Symphony No. 40 is in sonata form and belongs to a symphony.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
The two get sibling pages, Music/Form/Sonata and Music/Form/Sonata Form. Musicians already tell them apart that way in speech: "a sonata" and "sonata form."
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
A name that means one thing in both senses, such as fugue, gets one page.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
codekiln finds splitting the sonata from sonata form uncomfortable, and chose the sibling pages because they match how musicians talk.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures

Alternative: Music/Shape/. "Form" is overloaded and "shape" is not, so Music/Shape/Sonata and Music/Shape/Sonata Form keep the kind of piece apart from the music-theory sense. No one in music uses "shape" this way, so every reader would learn the term from the garden. A nested Music/Shape/Sonata/Form would also imply that sonata form is part of a sonata, which the Mozart example contradicts.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures

Alternative: Music/Genre/ for kinds of piece, Music/Form/ for structures. Musicologists use "genre" for the symphony, sonata and nocturne: Jim Samson's "Genre" article in Grove Music Online, Jeffrey Kallberg's "The Rhetoric of Genre: Chopin's Nocturne in G Minor" ( ), and Carl Dahlhaus on Gattung. The Library of Congress files "Preludes (Music)" and "Sonatas" among its Genre/Form Terms without choosing between the words. Working musicians call a sonata a form, not a genre, so the split reads as academic jargon.
One namespace for kinds of piece and structures
Genre means different things to different readers: a kind of piece to a musicologist, a style such as rock or ambient to most listeners.

codekiln would model a grouping like genre only if it worked the same way across literature, music and other disciplines of expression, and would prefer a neutral word such as "category." Form may face the same question across disciplines.
Works that organize music history by kinds of piece could change this. Dahlhaus's Nineteenth-Century Music and the Samson article are the places to start.
— Filed Logseq/Entity/Music/Form and with the first instance, Rachmaninoff's . Weighed Music/Shape/ and a genre/form split, kept Music/Form/ for both senses, and set genre aside.
A cross-discipline grouping word for kinds of works, and whether form belongs in it.
In this garden, Record Label pages model a label or imprint that releases music recordings.
A record label is the business or imprint named on a release. A label page collects the Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording pages it released.
An imprint with its own name and catalog gets its own page. It links its parent label with part-of:: when that label has a page.
A label that changes its name keeps one page, named for its current name, and its body lists the former names.
A recording studio, distributor, or publisher is a different thing from the label that released a recording.
Place a label at Label/<Name>, using the name printed on its current releases, as .

Check the exact page name, alias:: values, former names, the official domain, and plain-text mentions of the label on recording and person pages. A label mentioned only in prose on a recording page gets its page when it is filed.

A recording page links each of its labels with record-label::, defined at Logseq/Entity/Music/Recording/Frontmatter/record-label. Those links are the label's release list, so a label page lists recordings only to add notes about them.
Use founded-by:: for founders with person pages and part-of:: for a parent label.
Start each label page with logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Music/Label]] and one H1 with the label's name, linked to its official site.
